utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Laurie Sartorio, Matthias Neuner, Aditya Menon, and Kyle Wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to the colleagues from the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing General Delic with our legal assistants, Lejla Gluhic, Lana Deljkic, Asja Zulo, and our intern Claire Bonnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The purpose of today's session is to hear the closing arguments of the parties. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me begin by just briefly telling the Chamber the approach that the Prosecution will be taking with respect to closing arguments today. I will start with some very general comments concerning the questions put to the parties by the Trial Chamber. Mr. Menon will then address that part of indictment relating to the June 1993 crime base in Maline. That will be followed by Mr. Wood who will discuss the crime base concerning the July 1995 crimes; followed by Laurie Sartorio, who will be addressing the Chamber with respect to the September 1995 crime base. And we will then conclude with Matthias Neuner who will address general issues concerning command and control and indicators or indicia of effective control. Let me start by turning to the -- to the Trial Chamber's questions and specifically questions 1, 2, and 3. If we could please go to the PowerPoint presentation. Questions 1 and 2, as put by the Trial Chamber, will be addressed by Ms. Sartorio, and question number 3 will be addressed by Mr. Menon. Questions 5 and 8 will be addressed by Mr. Neuner, and I will address the Trial Chamber on the remaining questions. Question 4, the Trial Chamber asked what the significance of the presence of foreigners or Arabs within the ranks of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade; and, of course, this evidence was led pursuant to paragraph 24 of the indictment, which alleged that on the 8th of June, 1993, units of the 3rd Corps, including the 306th Mountain Brigade, 7th Muslim Brigade, and the Mujahedin launched an attack on Maline. The short answer to the question, as put by the Chamber, is that there was no evidence adduced at the trial that the 7th Muslim Brigade was involved in the attack on Maline on the 8th of June, 1993 as the Prosecution alleged. However, there was evidence that foreign fighters were in the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the Prosecution asserts that that clearly demonstrates that foreigners were not exclusively with the Mujahedin from Poljanice or subsequently in the El Mujahedin Detachment. And I will briefly run through a few of the exhibits that clearly indicate the presence of the foreign fighters within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Let me stress that the primary reason that that evidence was related to Maline, and there has been no evidence that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was involved in that attack. But, as I have indicated, it is important, we believe, in terms of the overall context of this case the evidence that relates to the presence of foreigners or Arabs within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade throughout the indictment period. Again, Exhibit 108 indicates that as at least as of the 15th of March, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had 1.439 soldiers. And in paragraph 2 of this document, there is reference to around 60 Arabs or Turks that were not included in the overall total numberless with respect to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade as of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You've told us that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was not involved in the Maline incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is not accused of having committed any other crimes in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In this indictment, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, it looks like -- I had asked that question, I'm quite satisfied with your answer, I don't think you need to go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honour. We'll then turn, if we can, to slide 20. The next question that I will addressing Your Honours on is question number 6, which indicates: Is it Prosecution's case that Rasim Delic had actual knowledge of the crimes allegedly occurring in 1995, or only that he had reason to know of these crimes? Your Honours, the Prosecution case is that the accused Rasim Delic had reason to know of the crimes allegedly occurring in 1995; although, there is evidence from which the Trial Chamber could infer that he had actual knowledge. The Celibici Appeals Chamber judgement, in paragraph 239, clearly states that the relevant information only needs to have been provided or available to the commander or, in the Celibici Trial Chamber's words, in the possession of the commander. It is not required, the Prosecution submits, that the commander actually acquainted himself with the information, merely that it has been provided to him or is otherwise available or in the possession of the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to deal with "available." Can you going back to that quotation from the Celibici case. Could we have that quotation from the Celibici case? I would like you to deal to what extent "provided or available to" is supposed to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will get to some evidence in just a moment, Your Honour; but, basically, the issue of "provided to" or "available to" or "in the possession of" would indicate reports that are being sent up the chain of command, and based upon the available evidence, for example, concerning bulletins or security reports that witnesses testified should have been made available to the top level of the ARBiH. That is information that was going up the chain of command which it would be reasonable to assume would be brought to the attention of the commanding officer and/or addressed to members of his staff, which, when fully functioning, would be in a position to make that information available to the commanding officer. There is also, for example, case law -- earlier case law from the hostage case which has been incorporated into the commentaries of Additional Protocol I by the ICRC, which states at paragraph 3545 of the Additional Protocol I commentary: It seems to be established that a superior cannot absolve himself from responsibility by pleading ignorance of reports addressed to him or by invoking temporary absence as an excuse. The issue of knowledge of the 1995 crimes is set forth in paragraphs 376 through 385 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. For example, in paragraph 376, the Prosecution sets forth citations to exhibits from ARBiH security bulletins, concerning the criminal activity of the El Mujahedin Detachment in August and September 1995. And as Your Honours will see on the screen - and, again, this is an extract from paragraph 376 - in the approximately 25-day period from 11 August 1995 through 4 September 1995, a number of security bulletins addressed criminal activity or criminal behaviour by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, including serious crimes and other misdemeanors on the 19th of August, 1995; physical abuse on the 26th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. It is one thing to say serious crimes and misdemeanours, it is quite another to state categorically what kind of crimes these are. Obviously, if it is a -- are these the kind of crimes that are justiciable in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this evidence goes to the fact of knowledge or inquiry knowledge or the need for the accused to make further inquiries concerning what is contained in these reports. So this issue goes to the point of inquiry type of notice that would put him on knowledge as to alleged criminal activities by this detachment in the period leading right up to the September 1995 crime base. And so we would submit that this goes very much to the point of knowledge and notice, and particularly inquiry notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am with you on that one. What I do want to know is: Is this knowledge of the type of crime that he is currently accused of, or is it just a question of you desecrated or the kind of crimes or misdemeanours that were mentioned, like harassing ladies in the streets, et cetera? Are these war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, there is, perhaps, no indication from these bulletins that these would rise to the level of war crimes. What we're simply stating is that this is a detachment which the accused knew and other members of the ARBiH and 3rd Corps knew had a propensity to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Turning to the next topic that we have addressed in the brief, and which I think needs to be stressed, is the fact that much of this informing concerning the capture of the prisoner of war and civilians by the El Mujahedin Detachment in September 1995 was publicly available. Exhibit 1194, the ARBiH publication Prva Linija for 1 October 1995 contains articles that deal with the combat activities in the period July through September 1995, making specific reference to the El Mujahedin Detachment, which, again, would tend to indicate that there might have been crimes committed. There's a reference, for example, to liquidation of Chetniks. Please go to the next slide. There is also clear reference to the fact that the El Mujahedin Detachment had captured Chetnik prisoners of war. Similarly, Exhibit 1195, the patriotic list edition of October 1995 makes reference to Chetnik officers taken prisoner. Now, given the evidence concerning the June 1993 crime base, which Mr. Menon will be talking about shortly, the fact that the Mujahedin from Poljanice whom the Prosecution asserts were the corps, if you will, the basis which the El Mujahedin Detachment was formed, from the very day the accused Rasim Delic assumed command of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was, of course, 15 years ago yesterday, he was on notice that this unit had a propensity to commit these types of crimes, and particularly crimes involving prisoners of war. So the simple fact that this public information, on top of security service bulletins, put him on notice, we would allege, that the El Mujahedin Detachment had prisoners of war, coupled with this propensity for that unit or members of that unit to commit crimes, should have put him on notice that something was amiss. We go to the next topic. Further information from the 3rd Corps concerning the capture of and crimes committed against prisoners of war and civilians in 1995. Exhibit 669 is an important piece of evidence. This is a document from the 3rd Corps sent up the chain of command, dealing with operation -- operative activities against the El Mujahedin Detachment and intelligence regarding that detachment. It was addressed to the ARBiH General Staff security administration. And attached to that this document, Exhibit 669, or being forwarded with it were two intercepted faxes from the 3rd Corps El Mujahedin Detachment. The second report that was part of this ARBiH 3rd Corps security report going up the chain of command clearly states the Mujahedin gained ground and entered a group of Serbian villages and took 60 prisoners after the killing. We would, again, assert that this document was one which would have been available to the accused, and the testimony of Dzemal Vuckovic, the head of the analysis and information affairs department in the military security administration of the General Staff, was asked some questions about this document. He clearly indicated, as reflected on page 5513 of the transcript, that this report was sent to us, meaning the Security Administration, by the 3rd Corps. And if we look also at his consolidated 92 ter statement, paragraph 57, he again makes reference to what was subsequently admitted as Exhibit 669 and stated this should have been reported to the top level, the same or next day. We would assert, Your Honours, that this clearly demonstrates the accused should have been on notice and perhaps had actual notice based upon this testimony that this document in particular should have been sent to the top level of the ARBiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution's position that once information has reached the Security Administration, then it meets the retirement of "available to" or "provided to"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, I will stress what I indicated at the beginning, which was that the Prosecution is primarily relying upon the notion that he had reason to know and was put on inquiry notice. However, based upon the totality of the evidence presented, including the evidence from persons such as Mr. Bukovic from the Security Administration, and other witnesses who have testified about how these types of reports were routinely handled, that the Trial Chamber can make the inference that this information was in the actual possession of the accused Rasim Delic, and, therefore, he had clear notice of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear that I understand and that we are on the same wave length in your response to my earlier question. In other words, once information reaches the administration, security administration services, irrespective of whether or not that is evidence of that information actually be given to the accused, that "provided to" and "available to" him as a retirement would be satisfied. That is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Information coming to the staff, the Main Staff, the General Staff of the ARBiH, is information, we would assert, is in the position or made available to the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now to question 7 which has two prongs. The first prong concerns continued reliance the El Mujahedin's contributions and whether or not that would constitute risk that further violations could be committed by that unit. In response to this question, the Prosecution will submit that continued reliance on the El Mujahedin Detachment's contributions, without taking any measures or further measures to monitor or discipline the members of that detachment, in fact does constitute acceptance of the risk that further violations would be committed by that unit. The issue of knowledge of past crimes was dealt with very recently by the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, and there the Appeals Chamber clearly states that knowledge of past crimes can put a superior on notice of the risk of future crimes. Turning to paragraph 30 of the Appeals Chamber judgement in Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, the Appeals Chamber clearly indicated that a case by case assessment would be necessary, and that a Trial Chamber may take into account the failure by a superior to punish the crime in question. The Appeals Chamber went on to state that such a failure is relevant to the determination of whether a superior possessed information that was sufficiently alarming to put him on notice of risk that similar crimes might be carried out by subordinates and justify further inquiry. And that, the Prosecution asserts, is the clearly the case presented by the facts in evidence in this proceeding. It is also important to look at the final sentence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're having a problem. There's cross-interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me repeat. It is also important to look at the final sentence of paragraph 30 of the Appeals Chamber judgement, which states the Appeals Chamber stresses that a superior's failure to punish a crime of which he was actual knowledge is likely to be understood by his subordinates at least as acceptance, if not encouragement much such conduct, with the effect of increasing the risk of new crimes being committed. That language from the Appeals Chamber is particularly important in this case, because, again, as will be seen by the comments of Mr. Menon in a few moments, following the crime in Maline and Bikosi on the 8th of June 1993 and the subsequent notice that was made available to the accused in June 1993, failure to take steps to discipline the Mujahedin from Poljanice who were involved in that crime, coupled with the fact that in August 1993, the accused ordered the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, which would included, we would submit, members of the Mujahedin from Poljanice, falls clearly within the scope of the final sentence of this paragraph. To be quite clear, we are not suggesting that knowledge of past crimes automatically puts a superior on notice of the risk of future crimes. As the Appeals Chamber has clearly said, a case by case assessment is necessary taking into account the facts of the case: Past crimes must have been committed in circumstances making it possible for the superior to foresee the recurrence of such crimes, thereby requiring him to take the steps necessary to address the risk. In this case, there are, the Prosecution's submits, three primary factors that the Trial Chamber should look at with respect to the issue of risk: The nature and extent of the detachment's prior criminal conduct, and we've talked about already this morning and it will addressed throughout the remainder of today; the general reputation and operating methods of the detachment; and the nature of the continued assignments given to the detachment, knowing of their prior conduct. We would submit that a superior who is on notice of a risk of future crimes is required to do more than simply making further inquiries. A superior who is on notice of a risk of future crimes must take the necessary and reasonable steps to prevent the future crime from occurring. And depending upon the circumstances, this may involve making additional inquiries and/or taking concrete steps to reduce the known risk of such crimes. In this case, as the Chamber is well aware, evidence was led that not only was the El Mujahedin Detachment, or the Mujahedin from Poljanice more specifically, involved in crimes of June of 1993, but criminal conduct and criminal activity continued throughout the indictment period. The Paul Godale murder being an example of criminal activity from January 1994, and Exhibit 658 relates to this crime. As a result of that, an operative plan was put in place. Exhibit 658 discusses the security assessment of the findings concerning that incident, being the murder of Paul Godale; and, of course, that document also indicates that the interviews were to be conducted of members of the detachment based on the established facts that the vehicle used by the murderers belonged to the El Mudjahedin unit. We would, again, submit that this constitutes risk, acceptance of risk, that members of this detachment were involved in, in this case, the Paul Godale case, killing of a humanitarian worker. But this information concerning criminal activities didn't stop in January 1994. It continued into 1995, when, in the words of witnesses, the security assessment and security situation concerning members of the El Mujahedin Detachment continued to be a problem. Exhibit 964 relates to what came to be known as Operation Vranduk. This document clearly indicates that the El Mujahedin Detachment had members whose behaviour is very suggestive from a security point of view. Similarly, this document, which was written by General Jaserevic from the Security Administration, makes reference to illegal activities and actions committed by some members of the detachment. As a result, General Jaserevic suggested establishing an operative action the El Mudjahedin Detachment, to include secret listening and recording, secret monitoring and observing, secret searches, and secret control of the mail. General Delic approved this plan, putting into place Operation Vranduk on the basis of the information contained in this exhibit. On the 15th of June 1995, as demonstrated by Exhibit 665, further information on intelligence from the El Mujahedin Detachment, addressed to the Main Staff Security Administration, there is more reference to crimes committed by -- by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, including the liquidation of a number of Chetniks. It's indicated in this document that two such persons were slaughtered and their heads carried throughout the villages down the Krivaja river, showing the heads to the locals and school children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were those two killed in combat, or were they just killed when they were not in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is unclear, Your Honours, from the document. However, what is more telling than the actual killings is the fact that these soldiers, whether killed in combat or subsequent to combat, apparently based on the document, had their heads decapitated and those heads were then paraded through local villages, to include being shown to school children. That is precisely the type of notice, whether those soldiers were killed in combat or not, that should have been extremely alarming when it reached the Security Administration of the Main Staff, and, therefore, was available, in our submission, to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document concludes by indicating that the Security Administration will continue to follow the conduct of the El Mujahedin unit members through operative work and subsequently make reports. Let me turn now to the second prong of question 7, which asked whether a referral by the 3rd Corps for investigation to the military or civilian prosecutor would meet the requirements of material ability to punish. Of course, the requirement of effective measures, which is the third element of superior responsibility, and the material ability to punish, the first element of superior responsibility, are flip sides, if you will, of the same coin. In order to have a superior subordinate relationship, one must have, or a commander must have, effective control, which means the material ability to prevent or punish. Superiors can only be held responsible when they take effective measures within one's material ability. In this sense, with respect to the question concerning referral, Exhibit 25, which is the order on district military courts is, in our submission, particularly informative on this point. Article 27 consists of three paragraphs. The second paragraph relates to what might be more colloquially known as referral: The military commander of the military unit institution is obliged to inform immediately the district military prosecutor or supreme commander about information referred in paragraph 1 of this article; paragraph 1, of course, being crimes. But it is interesting to note that this paragraph that talks about referral is the second paragraph of Article 27. The first paragraph of Article 27, which is displayed on the screen in front of you, also puts certain other obligations on military commanders: The commander of the unit and the military institution is obliged to make certain actions, so that the person who committed the criminal act, for which official prosecution is foreseen, does not hide or escape, and the traces and objects which may be used as evidence are preserved, and to collect all information that may be useful for conducting the criminal procedure. We would submit that simply referring the matter to the relevant district military prosecutor' office, in light of this statutory requirement, is insufficient, unless the steps taken contain in the first paragraph of Article 27 have also been fulfilled; that is, -- I see my colleague on her feet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise interrupting my colleague. I would just like to some receive guidance from you. If the Prosecutor is using a document that we objected to, rather, we objected to a erroneous translation, and we sought officially to have the translation corrected, and now this document is being placed before you as an exhibit as evidence, I think that this might mislead the Trial Chamber, and since this is something that has occurred several times in several important situations, whether it would be visible for me to seek it. For instance, here, the translation reads military commander; whereas, it should read senior officer, starijesne [phoen], in Bosnian. And this paints a completely different picture from what you get, and this is -- this goes beyond the context of what the Prosecutor is talking about. I do apologise for rising, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Was your objection upheld at the time you raised it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Moreover, afterwards, having seen that they are again using documents that we have made clear that they have been mistranslated, I again sought from the CLSS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mundis, apparently, you are using a document about which the Defence objected and about which the Chamber upheld the objection. Now, I have no recollection of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let me perhaps -- perhaps the best way to go forward would be if the registry could pull up Exhibit 25, and we'll just go to the version that has been available in e-court. It is possible that this exhibit -- I don't have a specific recollection of that either. It is possible that this exhibit, the translation was corrected and it simply wasn't uploaded into the systems that the Prosecution uses. That is certainly within the range of the possible. I'm happy for the registry to pull up the official version of Exhibit 25. And if we could go in that document to Article 27, I don't think it is going to make much of a point with respect to the point I'm talking, but I'm happy -- of course, the corrected version of the translation is the one we rely on; and if I have made an error, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Will the registry please help us with bringing up Exhibit 25 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I, obviously, stand corrected based on - it's Article 27 - the first and second paragraphs. I, obviously, stand corrected with respect to the version that I had put on the screen. But the point, Your Honours, is the same. The senior officer in a military unit or a military establishment shall take measures to prevent the perpetrator of a criminal offence from going into hiding or escaping. In other words, the point we're trying to make is that referral in the absence of taking the other measures, both to ensure the perpetrator does not escape or that the evidence of the criminal offence is not destroyed or otherwise lost, is an extremely important component that senior officers in military units or a military establishment must take; that is, a simple referral to a criminal court or a district military prosecutor's office may not be enough in situations where the perpetrators are allowed to escape and/or evidence is not properly collected. So, the point being that referral might be sufficient in cases where the military unit has taken the proper steps set forth in Article 27. But if those steps have not been taken, simply referring the event or alleged crime to a district military prosecutor' office is insufficient in and off itself, unless the steps envisioned by Article 27 are not taken. The final point I would make on this issue of referral, with respect to obligations of commanders, the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, at paragraphs 20 through 20.11, contain a very detailed explanation of the obligations of commanders. And we would refer Your Honours back to that document for additional information in that respect. At this point in time, Your Honours, I will turn the floor over to my colleague Mr. Menon, who will address you on the June 1993 crime base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My approach will be to focus on specific paragraphs from the -- from the Defence final brief, and to highlight evidence which we believe counters the arguments that the Defence have made. I begin at paragraph 194 of the Defence final brief, where the Defence state the military action in the Bila valley was a low intensity combat action, not a major operation. They say this was not an attack on the whole Bila valley, but rather focussed towards Velika Bukovica. We believe that the evidence shows otherwise. We believe the results which the ARBiH realized on the ground show that its focus was, in fact, on seizing control of the Bila valley. We see here Exhibit 1213, in relation to which Mr. Halim Husic, when asked which villages controlled villages by the ARBiH at the beginning of June 1993, he indicated that villages 1, 13, 2, 9, 5, 12, and 3 were controlled by the ARBiH. Your Honours, this would roughly correspond to half of the Bila valley; therefore, half of the valley at the beginning of June 1993 was controlled by the ARBiH and half of the valley was controlled by the HVO. We see Exhibit 1213 again, Your Honours, in relation to which Halim Husic, when asked which villages the ARBiH had control over after the 10th of June 1993, he indicated that all of the villages, at least the villages marked 1 to 14, were in the control of the ARBiH. In essence, Your Honours, after the 10th of June 1993, the ARBiH controlled the Bila valley. Whilst the Defence may claim that the ARBiH was not focussed on seizing control of the Bila valley, we would submit that the successes which they obtained through combat in the Bila valley betray the objectives that they had when they entered into that combat. We see here paragraph 193 from the Defence final brief, where they indicate that it can be concluded that the combat action in the Bila valley arose ad hoc based upon an immediate need for assistance and without any proper prior planning. We believe that the evidence shows that in the days prior to 8 June 1993, 3rd Corps commander Enver Hadzihasanovic was committed to undertaking military action in the Bila valley, and that he would not have done so unless the military action which followed was, in fact, planned. We see here, Your Honours, Exhibit 283, which is a BritBat document. The document speaks of a meeting on the 5th of June 1993, which involved amongst others the 3rd Corps Commander Hadzihasanovic and Witness Alistair Duncan. We see that the document reports that during that meeting, General Hadzihasanovic adopted an extremely hard line attitude throughout the meeting. And we see that, on the basis of that meeting, that BritBat concluded that the ARBiH were no longer prepared to retrain themselves and were, in fact, likely to take military initiative in the Lasva valley. Witness Alistair Duncan testified that the Bila valley was at the western end of the Lasva valley. We move on to the 6th of June 1993. Exhibit 284 speaks of two meetings that were held that day. Hadzihasanovic was supposed to attend the evening meeting but refused, maintaining his previous position that it was now too late for negotiation. BritBat concluded that the 3rd Corps, judging by the attitude of its commander, seems poised for further military action having clearly rejected the concept of negotiation. 8 June 1993, Your Honours. BritBat's predictions were confirmed. They reported that the expected BiH offensive in the area has begun, a major Muslim push is being made down the Bila valley. We believe, Your Honours, that the evidence leaves little to no doubt that the operation undertaken by the ARBiH on 8 June 1993 was, in fact, a planned affair. Paragraph 194, Your Honours, of the Defence final brief. They state in the last sentence: "In terms of the command and control over the parts of the 306 MB that set off from Mehurici, it was clear that Commander Sipic was unable to exercise any control as he was blocked Krpeljici. Your Honours, we believe this is a particularly important issue because the Prosecution has argued at paragraph 56 to 58 of its final brief that on 8 June 1993, the 306th Mountain Brigade carried out the order which is set out in Exhibit 258 and that they did so in conjunction with the Mujahedin combatants --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour, I will speak slowly. As I was saying, Exhibit 258, we have argued, contains an order which the 306th Mountain Brigade carried out in conjunction with the Mujahedin combatants from the Poljanice camp. This order had been issued to Esed Sipic, the 306th Brigade commander, by Alagic, the OG Bosanski Krajina commander. We see that, in Exhibit 258, the document speaks of connection with Sipic being interrupted. It goes on to state: "We do not have information if already on his way and how far he has come." We know, Your Honours, from Exhibit 284, that by the 6th of June 1993, Alagic and Sipic did, in fact, have contact. We see from Exhibit 284 that they both attended the meetings spoken of in that document. We believe, Your Honours, that this supports our argument that, in fact, the order in Exhibit 258 was carried out on 8 June 1993. Paragraph 204 of the Defence final brief, Your Honours, where the Defence claim that there is no proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Mujahedin were involved in the Maline attack or they were observed in the village. We see in front of us Exhibit 99, which was marked by witness Saban Alic. Mr. Alic was a member of the Mudjahedin from Poljanice on the 8th of June, 1993. He testified that a breakthrough group from the camp launched the attack. Saban Alic was in a combat group that followed the breakthrough group. In doing so, Saban Alic's group moved from point 3, which is marked as Simulje, to point 4, which corresponds with Borje. In doing so, he passed via point 5. We see that the path taken by the Mujahedin would have placed them in the area of Gornje Maline on the 8th of June, 1993. We see in front of us, Your Honours, Exhibit 132, which was marked by Zdravko Pranjes. He was an HVO soldier that was manning the line that was set up around Gornje Maline prior to the ARBiH attack on the 8th of June, 1993. He drew that line on Exhibit 132, and that is represented by the red line that Your Honours on the screen in front of you. The arrows on the screen represent the movement of the Mujahedin that day based on the evidence of Saban Alic. We see from this exhibit, Your Honours, that the Mujahedin clearly attacked the HVO line around Maline on the 8th of June, 1993, and that this, in fact, corroborates the testimony given by witnesses who saw Mujahedin fighters in the village of Gornje Maline on the 8th of June, 1993, following the Bosnian Croat surrender of that village. At paragraph 204 of the Defence final brief, the Defence take issue with the testimony given by Witness Zeljko Pulseja. The Defence claim that the Prosecutor asked a series of leading questions, which resulted in the witness describing two men with beards with dark skin and a third with black curly hair. The Defence are referring to observations that Mr. Pulseja made in Gornje Maline following the Bosnian Croat surrender of that village. Your Honours, we would submit that none of the questions asked of Mr. Pulseja were leading in any respect. The Defence cite to questions at pages 1029 to 1031 of the transcript. Rather than reading -- the questions are actually listed on the screen. I won't read them all out, but I would simple put it on the record that we do not consider any of those questions to be leading. And we ask that the Trial Chamber carefully exam those questions and carefully assess the Defence's argument on the basis of the questions that were asked. Paragraph 207 of the Defence final brief, Your Honours. Here, the Defence refer to Saban Alic's testimony to claim that there were no arrangements made with the ARBiH to participate in combat in the Bila valley. They quote Mr. Alic as saying: "I was a spontaneous thing and I simply joined in." Your Honours we would submit that Saban Alic was not in a position to know whether the Mujahedin had made arrangements to participate in combat with the ARBiH. Saban Alic joined the Mujahedin on 1 June 1993, a week prior to the operation. Furthermore, the evidence given by Saban Alic shows that he was merely a foot soldier within the ranks of the Mujahedin. We would submit that the appropriate witness to refer to on this point would be Witness Ali Hamad. Mr. Hamad served in the Mujahedin unit in Karaula from September 1992 until approximately November 1992. The unit that he was in -- the unit that he was in eventually left Karaula and moved to Bijelo Bucje. And while that unit was in Bijelo Bucje, Ali Hamad served as a deputy commander, and for approximately the first six months of 1993 as the commander. When asked at page 29 of the 7 September 2007 transcript, "As the deputy commander after that unit, can you tell the Trial Chamber how combat operations were planned and organised," he indicated that: "First, the senior officers of BiH arm would meet with commander in Mehurici. After that, I would receive orders from the Mujahedin command that I need to collaborate with the Bosniak units and take part in the attacks which they had proposed." We would submit that from his evidence, it is clear that the combat objectives were set by the ARBiH and communicated to Mujahedin fighters through the Mujahedin command. It is also apparent from Ali Hamad's testimony that Wahiddin, the Mujahedin military chief, would have allowed the Mujahedin to engage in combat without the authorisation of the ARBiH. In this respect, Ali Hamad testified, at pages 38 to 39 of the 7 September 2007 transcript, that: "I had to cooperate with the B and H army. We could not attack any location without asking them." Your Honours, we would submit that the only reasonable information inference to be drawn from this evidence is that the priorities for the combat undertaken by the Mujahedin in the Bila valley were communicated to the Mujahedin command by ARBiH commanders within the 3rd Corps. We would submit that it could not have been merely a random incident, as the Defence would have the Trial Chamber believe, that the Mujahedin from Poljanice engaged in combat from 8 June 1993. Paragraph 208 of the Defence final brief. Here, the Defence refer to Witness Sinan Begovic. And they state that he said that members of -- of the 306th Mountain Brigade, who were fighting in June, did not have clear information -- did not have any clear information about the involvement, if any, of the Mujahedin from Poljanice on -- in combat activities. The Defence here referred to combat activities on the 8th of June, 1993. We would submit that it is very clear from the evidence that Sinan Begovic did, in fact, know that the Mujahedin participated in the 8 June 1993 combat operation. When asked, at page 402 of the 11 July 2007 transcript, whether there were rumours that the Mujahedin were there or whether they were actually there, he testified that there were. That is unequivocal. They were in action. Furthermore, in line with the testimony given by Poljanice Mujahedin members Saban Alic and Hasib Alic, Sinan Begovic indicated that the Mujahedin moved from Simulje, point 3 on Exhibit 64, to point 2 on Exhibit 64, Borje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Menon, I need to follow in French. The interpreters are asking you, once again, to slow down just a bit, otherwise they cannot interpret accurately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour. I will endeavour to speak much more slowly. As I was saying, Begovic confirmed that the Mujahedin moved from point 3 to point 2, from Simulje to Borje. His unit moved parallel to the Mujahedin. They moved from Suhi Dol to Percin. And just for clarification, at that time, Begovic was a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade. We would submit that this exhibit can only show coordination, a high degree of coordination, between 306th Mountain Brigade and the Mujahedin from Poljanice. It is clear that they were coordinating their activities on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Paragraph 118 of the Defence final brief. Here, the Defence recount an episode during the Bila valley operation that took place at the Guca Gora church, and they do so to support the position that the Mujahedin were not under Mehmed Alagic's control. The incident itself was characterized by an attempt of a Mujahedin fighter to blow up the Guca Gora church over the objections of Mehmed Alagic. Contrary to what the Defence claim, we would submit that this episode is, in fact, an example of Mujahedin compliance with ARBiH instruction. We see from witness Ali Hamad's testimony, at page 117 of the 8 September 2007 transcript, that he clearly indicated that the chief of the Mujahedins accepted Alagic's order not to blow up the church in Guca Gora. Paragraph 228 of the Defence final brief. Here, the Defence assert that the Prosecution alleges that the Mujahedin came out of the Poljanice camp. The evidence does not show this at all. I would refer Your Honours to paragraphs 215 to 217 of the Prosecution's final brief, which set out the relevant facts that clearly show that the perpetrators of the crimes in Bikosi emerge from the area where the Poljanice camp was located, and that they then proceeded to separate the victims from those who were taken to the Mehurici school. Paragraph 230 of the Defence final brief, Your Honours. Here, the Defence refer to other groups, other Mujahedin groups, that it claims may have perpetrated the crimes in Bikosi. In this sense, the Defence specifically refer to Abu Hamza's group, the Zenica Gerila, and Abu Zebeir's group. We know, Your Honours, that the perpetrators were foreigners and Bosniaks, and that the Poljanice Mujahedin had both amongst its ranks. This is not in dispute. If we could go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: As I was saying, though the Defence claim, at paragraph 89 of their brief, that Abu Hamza's group was comprised of Bosnian and foreigners, the testimony to which they cite at that paragraph actually refers to the group at Poljanice and not Abu Hamza's group. The testimony to which they cite is specifically from Witness Aiman Awad's testimony. We would submit, again, that there is no evidence to suggest that Abu Hamza's group including locals amongst its ranks. Furthermore, Your Honours, it is it apparent from Asim Delalic's testimony that the 306th Brigade was aware that the perpetrators of the crimes in Bikosi were Mujahedin from the Poljanice camp. Specifically when asked, at pages 1710 to 1711, "Did you manage to establish the fate of these 20 to 25 missing," he answered: "The perpetrators were the Mujahedin." He then went on to claim that, "by virtue of the fact that I could not continue investigating, because in that period of time no one could enter the Mujahedin camp." From the question and answer exchange that we see on the screen in front of us, we know that Delalic was speaking of the Poljanice Mujahed because of the reference to the Mujahedin camp in Mehurici. We can trust the knowledge that existed within the 306th Mountain Brigade because the evidence shows that members of that brigade were, in fact, able to distinguish between different Mujahedin groups. Two examples, Your Honours, are relevant to this point. And, actually, Your Honours, I see that it is 10.15. Perhaps it is a good time to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break now and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe, when I left off, I was speaking of the ability of the 306th Mountain Brigade to distinguish between different Mujahedin groups, and there are two examples which we consider to be particularly relevant to this point. The first example relates to the Gerila. And at page 7308 of 11 March 2008 transcript, in relation to a theft committed in Guca Gora on the 8th of June, 1993, Halim Husic hesitated that: "Our policemen who were securing the monastery had already established that they were member of the Gerila from Zenica. We would submit that this shows that the military police of the 306th Mountain Brigade were able to establish the identity of this particular group and this particular and, therefore, able to distinguish between different Mujahedin groups. Abu Hamza's group, the second example. In relation to an incident of arson at Guca Gora church, Husic testified, at page 7306 to 7307 of the 11 March 2008 transcript, that the security service tried to investigate these events, and the young men who were charged with guarding these houses informed the police that the perpetrators was a group called Abu Hamza. Again, this shows that the 306th Mountain Brigade was able to distinguish between different Mujahedin groups. If we could please move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now one of the documents that reached the Main Staff in Sarajevo in the summer of 1993 after Delic's appointment as the Main Staff commander. We begin with Exhibit 179, which is a report from the 3rd Corps commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic, which was sent to the -- to Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic. It's dated 13 June 1993. It is not in dispute that this particular document reached Rasim Delic, and we know from that paragraphs 303 and 304 of the Defence final brief. Again, if we could move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exhibit 277, a 3rd Corps combat report, dated the 9th of August, 1993, which contains information relating to the El Jihad unit. We know that Exhibit 277 reached Rasim Delic because he reported information in that document to Alija Izetbegovic, and specifically the information relating to the El Jihad unit. He reported that information to Alija Izetbegovic on the 10th of August, 1993, and we see from that Exhibit 278. And, finally, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, I just wanted to check if there is identity between El Jihad and El Mujahid Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the evidence shows that prior to the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, it was commonly referred as the El Jihad unit amongst its own membership and within reports of the ARBiH. That is the state of the evidence on that point. Obviously, when it was formed, it was known as the El Mujahid Detachment, and I would refer Your Honours actually at this point to the formation video. I don't have the precise exhibit number, but it was tendered through Aiman Awad, where during the formation of the El Mujahid Detachment they had actually had a banner that said El Jihad, Brigada El Jihad. We have in front of us, Your Honours, Exhibit 272, which is the proposal to form the El Mujahid Detachment, dated the 12th of August, 1993, and it is not in dispute that Exhibit 272 reached Rasim Delic. We know that, obviously, because his handwriting appears on this document, as confirmed by witness Murat Softic, and the Defence have conceded that point at paragraph 314 of their brief. My point simply, Your Honours, is that if Exhibits 179, 168, 173, 174, 277, and 272 were available to Rasim Delic, each having had to go through Sefer Halilovic, the chief of the Main Staff, there can be no reasonable explanation as to why Exhibits 170 and 171 would not have been available to Rasim Delic as well. The only reasonable explanation, in our view, is that exhibits 170 and 171 were, in fact, available to Rasim Delic. At the paragraph 301 of the Defence final brief, they state that: "Because of Croat propaganda spread throughout Croatia and BiH, ARBiH commands including the Main Staff and the international community had no trust in information coming from Croat sources in Bosnia -- excuse me, in Central Bosnia." This would be appear to be an attempt on the part of the Defence to justify the accused's failure to act on the information that was contained in Exhibits 170 and 171. The Trial Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, at paragraph 1223 of their judgement, found that the source and content of information are to be considered in assessing whether a particular piece of information will satisfy the mens rea requirement under Article 7(3) of the Statute. May we move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed now, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: When President Izetbegovic wrote to Rasim Delic, he already had the information at his disposal from PW-3 as far as crimes committed in Bikosi. Now, at that point, he was -- Rasim Delic was obliged to carry out an investigation. Now, I understand that Your Honours' question relates to the information that Rasim Delic subsequently received as a result of that investigation. Is that correct? Well, we would submit that under the case law identified in Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, it would still have been incumbent upon Rasim Delic to have examined the information that was presented to him from Witness PW-3, because Witness PW-3 was a reliable source and information coming from him was trustworthy. He was still obligated to inquiry into that information, to see whether or not it was justified, whether or not there was a plausible bases for it. The investigation that he conducted did not relieve him of that obligation. That would be our position, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me be clear that I understand you. PW-3 reported to Rasim Delic the same incident that Izetbegovic reported to Rasim Delic. Okay. I understand that PW-3 reported it much earlier than Izetbegovic did. The gravamen of my question is, barring the fact that the investigation, as a result of the report from Izetbegovic, was conducted much later, does the fact that Rasim Delic did institute some kind of investigation and got a report, which may, on the face of it, might have been seen to answer even the queries raised by PW-3, does the Prosecution say that he was still enjoined to make further investigations over and above the investigation that he made as a result of Izetbegovic's letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on what basis does the Prosecution say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, we would submit, first of all, that the factual circumstances relating to the investigation that Delic carried out in October 1993 suggest it could have not been a real investigation. It was completed in a mere four days. That is the firs point. Secondly, PW-was adamant as far as the accuracy and reliability of his information. We would submit that Rasim Delic could not have simply ignored PW-3's appeals to him. Where a commander has conflicting information from reliable sources, the commander is obligated, in our view - and we believe that we're supported by the jurisprudence - to resolve these conflicts. In this case, Rasim Delic did not resolve this conflict, as it relate to the information that he received from Witness PW-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's be on the same wave length. My recollection is that the information from Izetbegovic did not conflict with the information from PW-3. It is the result of the investigation as a result of the instructions from Izetbegovic that came up with the result that differs with allegations by both Izetbegovic and PW-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exactly. And that is the point that I'm trying to make. Because of the conflict in the information that Delic subsequently received from the 3rd Corps, because of the nature of that conflict as it related to the information that he had previously received from Witness PW-3, we would submit that he was still obligated to inquire into the information that he received from PW-3. He could not simply have ignored that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I'm saying to you is: What he did receive from the 3rd Corps was not information, was not a report of an incident, it was the results of an investigation. In other words, the 3rd Corps was saying to him, "We've heard the allegations by Izetbegovic, we have heard the allegations by PW-3, we have conducted an investigation, and we have found out that, in fact, those allegations were unfounded because we find our investigations reveal that these people died in combat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have that redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: We would submit that because of the nature of that conflict between the information that he received from PW-3, not on just one occasion, on multiple occasions, that Rasim Delic was obligated as a responsible commander to inquire with PW-3 as to the veracity of his information. Your Honour, now I wanted to simply address question number 3 that Your Honours had put to the parties, and question 3 was: "On what exact based does the Prosecution allege the Mujahedin from the Poljanice camp were subordinated to Rasim Delic on 8 June 1993? " We would submit, Your Honours, that on 8 June 1993, when Rasim Delic became the Main Staff commander, the Poljanice Mujahedin were a de facto unit of the 3rd Corps; and, thus, they were indirectly subordinated to Rasim Delic through his authority over the 3rd Corps commander. That would be our answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what are the factors that indicate the de facto subordination of this group to the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would refer you to the numerous instances of joint combat in which the Poljanice Mujahedin engaged in from the time of their arrival in the RBiH. We know that when they arrived, they were first integrated into the Travnik Muslim Forces. And following the formation of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, they engaged in joint combat operations with that unit in Bijelo Bucje. They then engaged in joint combat operation in December 1992, to lift the -- to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. And throughout 1993, throughout the first six months of 1993, they continued to engaged in joint combat with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We know, from the evidence given by witness Ali Hamad, that in terms of the objectives that were set for them, during those joint combat operations, those objectives emanated from the ARBiH, and we saw that in respect of the 8 June 1993 operation as well. And we would submit that where the ARBiH is setting the combat priorities for the Mujahedin that that is a sufficient indication of subordination. That would be your argument in that suspect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Lattanzi has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Menon, what factor, additional factor, can you give us to talk about a joint operation? How can you explain the de facto subordination? Can you give us some more examples of de facto subordination of joint operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it really a question of, in terms of combat, first, who sets the priorities? And in this case, we would submit that the ARBiH set the priorities for the Mujahedin from Poljanice. Then there is the question of whether there was reporting before, during, and after; and we believe that in this case there was certainly reporting, and we have Ali Hamad's testimony to support that point. He specifically referred to reporting prior to, during, and after combat operations with Mehmed Alagic, who is the OG Bosanski Krajina commander. And, certainly, we would submit that that indicates that the Mujahedin were very much within the control of the ARBiH. Their movements were reported, and the ARBiH knew what actions they were taking. There was little that was done that was outside of the scope of what the ARBiH intended for the Mujahedin. And we would also submit, Your Honours, that on the 8th of June 1993, the Poljanice Mujahedin, the evidence shows, was a very small unit, and it is simply implausible to expect that they would haven been able to engage in these combat without coordinating their activities with neighbouring units, and without receiving instructions as to what to do from superior ABiH authorities. We would add that as a further illustration of the fact that they were, in fact, de facto subordinated or de facto within the compensation of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give numbers? You say they were a small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Actually no, Your Honour. I believe that evidence shows that it was approximately 40 to 50 fighters within that -- within the unit at that time; but, regrettably, I don't have a specific number or reference to provide to Your Honours. Your Honours, may have I a moment to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, now I would turn the floor over to my colleague Mr. Wood, who will be presenting on the July 1995 crime base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Menon. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: General Delic makes a number of assertions regarding the events in Livada and the Kamenica camp in July /August 1995. Most of these, as Your Honours are aware, are adequately addressed in the Prosecution's final brief and need not be rehashed here. Others are so lacking in merit that they are unworthy, in the limit the time available here, of a detailed response from the Prosecution, and I refer specifically to the assertion set forth in paragraphs 418 to 423 of the Defence closing brief, that Gojko Vujic is a POW who is somehow responsible for his own death in the Kamenica camp, for cursing in his agony near a man with a gun. I do, however, want to take a few moments to answer the assertions regarding the murders of Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic. These are charged in paragraph 33 of the amended indictment, which you see on the screen in front of you. General Delic makes a number of assertions about these murders; specifically, he says: There is no evidence to establish that the corpse and head of Predrag Knezevic was exhumed at Bozici. There is no conclusive evidence of where the men were who killed. There is no proof that the men were hors de combat when they were killed or that they were not killed in combat. There is no evidence as to who killed the men or the circumstances rounding their deaths, and there is no evidence as to the mens rea of the unknown perpetrators. Let's start with the that first Defence assertion first; that is, the body of Predrag Knezevic was not exhumed at Bozici. Now, the evidence, Your Honour, says otherwise. We know that the body of Predrag Knezevic, as well as that of Momir Mitrovic, was exhumed at Bozici. We know this from two exhibits, Exhibit 1174 and Exhibit 644. Let's start with Exhibit 1174. This exhibit contains the report of an exhumation that was conducted on 16 May 2006 in the locality of Mount Ozren, Bozici. One of the bodies recovered there was given a number, DNK-BL-878. After that body was exhumed, samples were taken and sent to the ICMP, which is the International Commission For Missing Persons, for DNA analysis. They produced a report using - if we could go to the next - that same number, as we can see on this slide, Your Honours. Now, here, we see a close-up of Exhibit 644, at least the top half of that, which is a DNA report. From this report, we can see that the IC MP tested a sample from BL-878. The ICMP tested this sample against family members of Predrag Knezevic, who provided DNA samples of their own. ICMP scientists found that BL-878 are the mortal remains of Predrag Knezevic. So we can see, Your Honours, that Predrag Knezevic was, in fact, exhumed at Bozici. We can follow the same evidence to see that Momir Mitrovic was also exhumed at Bozici. First, we see a report of exhumation, also in Exhibit 1174. We can see that this body was also exhumed at Bozici also on 16th May 2006. We can also see from a later page in the same report, that the body was assigned the number DNK-BL-877. Let's remember that number. Similarly, the ICMP scientists tested this sample, ran those results through its database and found that BL-877 is Momir Mitrovic. We can see from the evidence, Your Honours, that these two men, Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic, were exhumed at Bozici in 2006. Now, obviously, Momir Mitrovic and Predrag Knezevic are not here to tell us what happened it them on 21 July 1995, but these reports of their exhumations tell us a great deal about the circumstances surrounding their deaths. These reports also refute many of General Delic's further assertions. Now, what do these reports tell us? First of all, they tell us that these men were bound when they were killed. Now, this is from the exhumation report for Mitrovic. And we can see in the highlighted portion, during the exhumation, a green rope tied with nooses around the hands was found on the body; and, here, we see a picture of the nooses from the actual exhumation report, which is entered into evidence, Your Honours. As to Knezevic, the report notes, as you can see on the screen in front of you, that during exhumation, thin electrical cables tide with nooses around hands and legs were found on the body. And, here, we see a photograph of that wire, which is also from the exhumation. Now, as to Knezevic, this can also be seen from another photo in his exhumation file, which is again at Exhibit 1174. Now I want to draw your attention particularly to the left side of this photo. You can see on the screen in front of you there's the box. If we can just click. You can see, Your Honours, how these cables were found tied around the limbs of Knezevic. The fact that these men were bound when they died tells us that they were plainly hors de combat, that they were killed after they had been detained and not in combat. We can also see from the reports of exhumations, Your Honours, that one of the bones in the neck of Mitrovic was smoothly split with a sharp object. And, here we, see a picture of that vertebrae. You see the two halves of it, and the arrows indicate how they were cut. This is consistence with the testimony of the witnesses to this crime, who describe seeing the heads of these two men in the village of Livada, on 21 July 1995, and we will hear more about them in a moment. Finally, these reports also provide clues about where the men were killed. As I explained, these bodies were found in Bozici, which is less than two kilometres from Livada. Here, we see a cutout from the exhumation report, indicating the mark where the people who conducted the exhumation indicated where the bodies were found. Now the Prosecution has taken Map 15 from the Court binder and rendered it in three dimensions. We can see it moving on the screen there, to show the topography between the two villages and their close proximity. Now additional evidence also tells us that these men were killed in Livada, specifically the testimony of Dr. Branko Sikanic and Velibor Trivicevic. First, Dr. Sikanic. In his report, Dr. Sikanic notes that sometime during the evening before dusk, two heads of Serb soldiers were brought, and there was fresh blood dripping from the heads. Now, Dr. Sikanic, of course, is a medical doctor, which we know from his statement. Now, this testimony is consistent with what Velibor Trivicevic, who is also trained as a medic, said in his live testimony before the Tribunal. He told the Trial Chamber on 4 October 2007, at transcript 3673: "I was crystal clear in my statement. The heads that were brought into that room were still gushing blood all over the ground, all over our legs." Now, this is an important detail Trivicevic told the Trial Chamber because it shows that the men had to have been killed very close to the house in which Trivicevic and Dr. Sikanic were being held. He continued: "This had been done somewhere along the front line, and it had taken them 15 to 20 minutes to get me there from the front line. If they had arrived all the way from the front line, I don't know how much blood would have still been left in those heads to gush forth like that." A few moments later in his testimony, Trivicevic reiterated what he said, telling the Trial Chamber: "The fair thing to say would be this: I'm certain that they had not been killed at the front line and then brought over. As I said, there was blood dripping from those severed heads, and those heads had obviously been freshly severed." From this -- from this evidence, the Trial Chamber can infer that the men were killed in close proximity to the house in Livada, sometime near dusk, as Dr. Sikanic said, on 21 July 1995. This factor is important in answering General Delic's remaining assertions regarding these men, the identity of the killers and their intent. As I have explained for Your Honours, the evidence shows that Mitrovic and Knezevic were bound when they were killed, and we know from the witnesses and from the forensic evidence that they had been beheaded. The testimony also shows that, at the time of the beheading, there was a commotion in front of the house. Velibor Trivicevic explained this: "You could hear shouting and noise in front of the house. I didn't what was happening, with shouts of "Allah-u-ekber." One of the Mujahedin, who was guarding us, ran out of the room; and, very quickly, he came back to the room where we were, carrying in his arms the cut-off head of a person who I knew before. His name was Momir Mitrovic." You put the facts together, Your Honours, and a picture emerges of the execution of two Bound POWs. The Trial Chamber can infer from these facts that the men were killed by decapitation, which is, by definition, a very deliberate act. As to the identity of the killers, the Trial Chamber can infer from the evidence that members of the El Mujahid Detachment, ARBiH soldiers as alleged in the amended indictment, were the perpetrators of these killings. First, we know that these murders were committed in Livada at dusk on 21 July 1995. Now what does the evidence tell us about the situation in Livada on that day? It tells, Your Honours, us that Livada was an ARBiH village. We know, for example, from Exhibit 449 that the 35th Division ARBiH had an IKM, or a forward command post, in Livada; and this, of course, is dated 16 July 1995. We also know from ARBiH documents that the EMD, the El Mujahid Detachment, had members in Livada at that time. As the Trial Chamber might recall, the exhibit here, Exhibit 553, deals with, among others, Sikanic and Trivicevic, dated 22 July. It shows that the interviews with certain men, "Chetnik soldiers," it says, was carried out with the permission of El Mujahid members. Finally, the manner of the deaths of these men tells us something about their killers. The practice of beheading is a behaviour that is consistent with the El Mujahid Detachment, as the evidence shows. For example, as we heard earlier from today's presentation, from Exhibit 665, the Trial Chamber heard evidence that members of the El Mujahid Detachment had "liquidated a number of Chetniks, slaughtered two and carried their heads down the Krivaja river. And as noted earlier, this is June 1995, roughly a month before the beheadings there Livada. Also, of course, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that a member of the El Mujahid Detachment killed and beheaded Gojko Vujic in the Kamenica camp just three days later on 24 July 1995. Now, certainly the evidence shows there were other people in Livada on 21 July 1995, including women who beat the POW with a sticks, and a boy who kicked Krstan Marinkovic in the face, breaking his nose. You have heard testimony about that, Your Honours. Though this violence certainly constitutes cruel treatment, it does not come close in intensity for violence required for a beheading; rather, beheading is an act more consistent with a member of the El Mujahid Detachment than with any other people present in Livada on that day. From this evidence, Your Honours, we can see from that the Defence is wrong to assert that there is no evidence to establish that the corpse and head of Predrag Knezevic was exhumed at Bozici. We can see that the Defence is wrong to assert that there is no conclusive evidence of where the men were killed. We can see that the Defence is wrong to assert that there is no proof that the men were hors de combat when they were killed, or that they were not killed in combat. We can see that the Defence is wrong to assert that there is no evidence as to who killed the men or the circumstances surrounding their deaths. And the Defence is wrong to assert that there is no evidence as to the mens the mens rea of the unknown perpetrators. Rather, Your Honours, the evidence leads to only one reasonable inference: Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic were murdered by ARBiH soldiers, members of the El Mujahid Detachment on 21 July 1995; that the men were detained when they were killed; and that their killers acted with intent to cause their deaths. That concludes my presentation, Your Honours, and I will pass the microphone to my colleague, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. My presentation this morning will address the points raised in the Defence brief that pertain to the crimes alleged in Counts 1, 2, and 4, specifically the cruel treatment and/or murder of two groups of VRS prisoners of wars and the cruel treatment of three civilian women at the hands of the El Mujahid Detachment in September of 1995. As this Chamber is aware, the events leading up to those crimes began on the 11th of September, 1995, with the capture of a large group of VRS soldiers and Serb civilians who had been fleeing as a result of a major military offensive launched by the ARBiH against Serb forces, the previous day, in the Ozren-Vozuca region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, will you please go a little slower than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
